messages.subject: Re: NA MargLogLik and low BGammaHat
messages.body_plain:
Thank you!

Setting priors are too complex for my model. So, I have to leave it for now. I am exploring another model with moderation. But got errors:
Chain 1: Exception: Exception: invese_spd: LDLT factor failed   (in 'model_stanmarg' at line 384)
  (in 'model_stanmarg' at line 1835)

Chain 2: Exception: Exception: invese_spd: LDLT factor failed   (in 'model_stanmarg' at line 384)
  (in 'model_stanmarg' at line 1835)

How to solve this?

Best,
Yuan

在2023年8月20日星期日 UTC+2 18:37:21<Ed Merkle> 写道：
>
> Yuanyuan,
>
> A couple additions to Mauricio's response:
>
> I imagine that you have multiple slopes in your model, and the dpriors() thing sets a prior distribution for all slopes. So you might want to use prior() inside the model specification syntax. See:
>
> https://ecmerkle.github.io/blavaan/articles/prior.html#individual-parameters
>
> About ppmc() taking a long time: this partly depends on your model. If you have many columns in your data and/or missing data, it will take longer. I believe that future::plan("multicore") can help here (or "multisession" on windows), but it might still take awhile.
>
> Ed
>
>
> On Wed, 2023-08-16 at 07:44 -0700, Yuanyuan Hu wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi Mauricio,
> > > >
> > > I am exploring the influence of priors. Some follow-up questions for
> > > > weakly informative priors:
> > > > 1. Specific priors for RI-CLPMs: do you have any recommendations on
> > > > the values?
> > > > e.g., NcNeish
> > > > (2019; [https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657](https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657) <https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657%5D(https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657)> suggested:
> > >
> > > > "Two-Level Dynamic Structural Equation Models with Small Samples
> > > > assuming stationarity, the magnitude of the autoregressive inertia
> > > > paths from the outcome at time t – 1 to the outcome at time t must
> > > > fall between −1 and 1"
> > > > "Inertia Slope Variance.—The inertia slope of the outcome (y at time
> > > > t) autoregressed on the outcome at the immediately preceding time (y
> > > > at time t – 1) cannot exceed 1, provided that the assumption of
> > > > stationarity has been met."
> > > >  *
> > > >  *
> > > > 2. How to set these specific priors in blavaan?
> > > > E.g., dp=dpriors(XX) , to specify Inertia Slope Variance (0,1)
> > > > and autoregressive effect (-1, 1), what should XX be replaced?
> > > >
> > > 3. How to do the posterior predictive checking?
> > > > I tried the following code, but it took forever and still did not
> > > > give any output...
> > > > AFIs <- ppmc(fit.RICLPMEnjEff, thin = 10, fit.measures =
> > > > c("srmr","chisq","rmsea","cfi"))
> > > > summary(AFIs)
> > > > Can we do something in blavaan that is similar to posterior
> > > > predictive checking on the following website?
> > > > [https://utrechtuniversity.github.io/BayesianEstimation/content/wednesday/prior_posterior_predictive_practical.html](https://utrechtuniversity.github.io/BayesianEstimation/content/wednesday/prior_posterior_predictive_practical.html) <https://utrechtuniversity.github.io/BayesianEstimation/content/wednesday/prior_posterior_predictive_practical.html%5D(https://utrechtuniversity.github.io/BayesianEstimation/content/wednesday/prior_posterior_predictive_practical.html)>
> > > >
> > > Best,
> > > > Yuan
> > >
> > > > 在2023年4月3日星期一 UTC+2 14:25:55<[mauga...@gmail.com](mailto:mauga...@gmail.com)> 写道：
> > > > > > Yuan
> > > > > > >
> > > > > With MCMC the results will change a little bit between runs, due to
> > > > > MCMC error variability but should not change a lot.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > The main difference is due to not be running the same model, as you
> > > > > have different number of parameters.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > First, check between models and find what are the differences
> > > > > between them. Probably the fixed.x argument, you can give the same
> > > > > argument to blavaan and see if you get the same model. Can run it
> > > > > with very few iterations, just to see you have the right model.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > Once you have the same model, I would recommend BSEM with weakly
> > > > > informative priors, these are good general applications for small
> > > > > sample sizes. Can get properly estimated models, that dont rely on
> > > > > the large sample assumption
> > > > > > >
> > > > >

> >
> > Yuanyuan,
> >
> > A couple additions to Mauricio's response:
> >
> > I imagine that you have multiple slopes in your model, and the dpriors() thing sets a prior distribution for all slopes. So you might want to use prior() inside the model specification syntax. See:
> >
> > https://ecmerkle.github.io/blavaan/articles/prior.html#individual-parameters
> >
> > About ppmc() taking a long time: this partly depends on your model. If you have many columns in your data and/or missing data, it will take longer. I believe that future::plan("multicore") can help here (or "multisession" on windows), but it might still take awhile.
> >
> > Ed
> >
> >
> > On Wed, 2023-08-16 at 07:44 -0700, Yuanyuan Hu wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hi Mauricio,
> > > > >
> > > > I am exploring the influence of priors. Some follow-up questions for
> > > > > weakly informative priors:
> > > > > 1. Specific priors for RI-CLPMs: do you have any recommendations on
> > > > > the values?
> > > > > e.g., NcNeish
> > > > > (2019; [https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657](https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657) <https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657%5D(https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1578657)> suggested:
> > > >
> > > > > "Two-Level Dynamic Structural Equation Models with Small Samples
> > > > > assuming stationarity, the magnitude of the autoregressive inertia
> > > > > paths from the outcome at time t – 1 to the outcome at time t must
> > > > > fall between −1 and 1"
> > > > > "Inertia Slope Variance.—The inertia slope of the outcome (y at time
> > > > > t) autoregressed on the outcome at the immediately preceding time (y
> > > > > at time t – 1) cannot exceed 1, provided that the assumption of
> > > > > stationarity has been met."
> > > > >  *
> > > > >  *
> > > > > 2. How to set these specific priors in blavaan?
> > > > > E.g., dp=dpriors(XX) , to specify Inertia Slope Variance (0,1)
> > > > > and autoregressive effect (-1, 1), what should XX be replaced?
> > > > >
> > > > 3. How to do the posterior predictive checking?
> > > > > I tried the following code, but it took forever and still did not
> > > > > give any output...
> > > > > AFIs <- ppmc(fit.RICLPMEnjEff, thin = 10, fit.measures =
> > > > > c("srmr","chisq","rmsea","cfi"))
> > > > > summary(AFIs)
> > > > > Can we do something in blavaan that is similar to posterior
> > > > > predictive checking on the following website?
> > > > > [https://utrechtuniversity.github.io/BayesianEstimation/content/wednesday/prior_posterior_predictive_practical.html](https://utrechtuniversity.github.io/BayesianEstimation/content/wednesday/prior_posterior_predictive_practical.html) <https://utrechtuniversity.github.io/BayesianEstimation/content/wednesday/prior_posterior_predictive_practical.html%5D(https://utrechtuniversity.github.io/BayesianEstimation/content/wednesday/prior_posterior_predictive_practical.html)>

messages.subject: Re: NA MargLogLik and low BGammaHat
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mauricio,

I attached my code here and datafile (via WeTransfer, it's too big to attach here). The mdoerator is sex (binary: 1=male, 0=female). The predictor is my intervention (multicategorical, 3 groups, 0=neutral state, 1=enjoyment, 2=frustration). The outcomes are Enj, Eff, postTest, game. The model works under lavaan, but got the errors under blavaan.

The code for moderation:

RIEnj ~ d1*sex1
RIEnj ~ m11*sex1:group1 + m12*sex1:group2
RIEff ~ d2*sex1
RIEff ~ m21*sex1:group1 + m22*sex1:group2

Best,

Yuan

> > > A couple additions to Mauricio's response:

> > > I imagine that you have multiple slopes in your model, and the dpriors() thing sets a prior distribution for all slopes. So you might want to use prior() inside the model specification syntax. See:

> > >
> > > About ppmc() taking a long time: this partly depends on your model. If you have many columns in your data and/or missing data, it will take longer. I believe that future::plan("multicore") can help here (or "multisession" on windows), but it might still take awhile.

The ":" operator appears to work in blavaan for simple examples. I am suspecting that the model specification syntax is problematic here, especially because lavaan is also having non-positive definite covariance matrices.

I would advise to fit simpler versions of the model and work your way up to the full model. For example, it seems that you could start with a measurement model that excludes some of the regressions and lagged effects and within-person centering. Then re-add them once you are happy that the simpler model is working ok. You might also be able to make use of the new two-level functionality in blavaan 0.5-1, because it looks like you are using a random intercept.

Ed

messages.subject: Specifying beta priors on theta
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am running a model based on McArdle and Prindle's paper: A latent change score analysis of a randomized clinical trial in reasoning training <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19140642/>

I standardised my variables to help with convergence. I am getting some issues with the covariance matrix on theta being neither diagonal nor constrained, for which it was recommended that I read  https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08667, which I have done.

One recommendation is to apply beta priors on individual correlations, after transforming beta from 0,1 to -1,1. This discussion here in this blavaan Google Group suggests that this transformation on beta is implemented automatically
Setting uniform prior on specific error covariance <https://groups.google.com/g/blavaan/c/iy5BYF3ygBs/m/Dp4MbDexCAAJ> : "So you have to use a distribution with support between 0 and 1 (typically beta distribution), which is then automatically translated to a distribution with support on (-1,1). "

In this discussion, Ed Merkle recommends using a beta distribution where most of the density lies between 0.4 and 0.6, so that the prior should be "prior("dunif(.4,.6)")". As I have no reason not to apply this prior to my entire theta matrix, I tried the following: dp

=dpriors(theta= "dunif(.4,.6)")

but get the following error: "Error in dpriors(theta = ("dunif(.4,.6)")) : blavaan ERROR: JAGS distributions sent to dpriors(), but target != 'jags' (I am also confused as to why this is using JAGS distributions, when I haven't specific JAGS; I thought blavaan uses stan defaults).

Another option I tried was to set a gamma prior on the theta parameter of 0.37,05, because variance distributions tend to be chi-squared, while the mean of the chi-square distributions tends to follow a gamma-distribution, at least at lower n.
For gamma distributions, apparently you specify (df, 0.5).
To calculate df, apparently you use (n - p)*0.5/n), where n = sample size (n=55 or 60 for me, depending on the group) and p = number of parameters being estimated. To calculate the number of parameters estimated, I added up all intercepts and latent and regression parameters being estimated (I counted only 1 where they were constrained across time, providing the same estimate), which equalled 16
Applying this, I got df=55-16*0.5/55, arriving at 0.3545, and then for n=60, 0.3667.

messages.body_plain:
Belinda,

In theory, it seems like you could change the intercept priors to have a smaller SD. And the default priors in blavaan do not necessarily work well for all datasets. It often helps to set priors based on parameter values that you know are implausible, as opposed to previous research.

Looking at the intercepts in your output, though, it seems like some posterior intervals are very wide. The intercepts of NC and FC have posterior distributions that look similar to the priors, suggesting something isn't quite right about the model specification. Looking at the syntax, I am wondering about the lines like this:

> NC =~ 0*N0 + 0*N1

I am not sure that the "0*" should be there, because those are fixing the loadings to 0. I don't know the model well enough to know what is intended there, but maybe remove the "0*" part?

Ed

messages.subject: Re: Specifying beta priors on theta
messages.body_plain:
Hi Belinda,

Here are a few things related to your email. It looks like you are doing some good work, and some of the issues that you are encountering are inherently tricky in Bayesian modeling.

About the covariance matrix being neither diagonal nor constrained: you can't fix this issue with priors. If you want the message to go away, you could remove/comment out the following lines:

FC ~~ NC

brief_gec_1 ~~ brief_gec_2
#mean_sdq_1 ~~ mean_sdq_2
osari_ssrt_60ms_1 ~~ osari_ssrt_60ms_2
ant_conflict_1 ~~ ant_conflict_2

Then your model covariance matrices would be diagonal. But you might want to keep those lines because your theory/expectations tell you that you should keep those lines. In this case, it will be difficult to compute the Bayes factor for the reasons described in that article. I do not see an easy way out of that predicament. You could use the automatic Bayes factor computations and hope that one model is preferred so much, it doesn't matter whether the Bayes factor is off by a certain amount. You could move to WAIC or LOOIC. Or you could do something more involved to approximate the actual prior distribution, which would be similar to what is done in that paper but is also complicated.

And about uniform priors:

The "dunif(.4,.6)" syntax is JAGS syntax, which is why blavaan complains about JAGS. Also, the "theta" entry is for residual standard deviations, and you want to use "rho" to specify priors on correlations. So you would end up with something like

dpriors(rho = "beta(5,5)")

where the "5,5" could change depending on what you want. I would not want to use uniform here because it imposes hard cutoffs of possible values for the correlation parameters.

Ed
